from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Set seed for deterministic randomness in dot placement
        np.random.seed(42)
        
        title = "Prerequisite: The Concept of a Population vs. Sample"
        lines = [
            "A population represents every individual in a group.",
            "A sample is just a small portion of them.",
            "Real-world populations often have jagged, non-normal shapes."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_POP = WHITE
        COLOR_SAMPLE = "#58C4DD"
        COLOR_PARAMS = "#FFFF00"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Visual: Draw a large cluster of white dots representing the 'Population'.
        
        # Create a group of dots to represent the population
        dots = VGroup(*[
            Dot(radius=0.05, color=COLOR_POP, fill_opacity=0.6)
            for _ in range(80)
        ])
        
        # Randomly position dots in a cluster-like cloud
        for d in dots:
            angle = np.random.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
            dist = np.sqrt(np.random.uniform(0, 1.5))
            d.move_to([dist * np.cos(angle), dist * np.sin(angle), 0])
            
        # Position the population cluster in the grid area B2-E5
        self.place_in_area(dots, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        pop_label = Text("Population", font_size=24, color=COLOR_POP)
        self.place_at_grid(pop_label, "B2", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(COLOR_POP),
            LaggedStart(*[FadeIn(d) for d in dots], lag_ratio=0.01),
            Write(pop_label),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Visual: Circle a small subset of dots (#58C4DD) and label it 'Sample'.
        
        # Reset previous line color and highlight current
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        
        # Circle parameters
        sample_center = self.grid["C3"]
        sample_circle = Circle(radius=0.7, color=COLOR_SAMPLE, stroke_width=4)
        sample_circle.move_to(sample_center)
        
        sample_label = Text("Sample", font_size=24, color=COLOR_SAMPLE)
        # Position label close to the circle (within 1 grid unit)
        self.place_at_grid(sample_label, "C2", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Identify dots within the circle to change their color
        sample_dots = VGroup()
        for d in dots:
            if np.linalg.norm(d.get_center() - sample_center) < 0.7:
                sample_dots.add(d)
        
        self.play(
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE),
            Create(sample_circle),
            Write(sample_label),
            sample_dots.animate.set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE).set_fill(opacity=1.0),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Visual: Display μ and σ labels (#FFFF00) and a jagged distribution plot.
        
        # Reset previous line color and highlight current
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        
        # Parameter labels - Switched to Text to avoid dependency on system LaTeX installation
        mu_label = Text("μ (Mean)", font_size=24, color=COLOR_PARAMS)
        sigma_label = Text("σ (Std Dev)", font_size=24, color=COLOR_PARAMS)
        
        self.place_at_grid(mu_label, "E3", scale_factor=0.7)
        self.place_at_grid(sigma_label, "E4", scale_factor=0.7)
        
        # Jagged distribution plot to visualize "non-normal shapes"
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[0, 10, 1],
            y_range=[0, 5, 1],
            x_length=3,
            y_length=2,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "color": COLOR_PARAMS}
        )
        # Scale down as it is in the bottom-right extreme (Row F, Col 6)
        self.place_in_area(axes, "D4", "F6", scale_factor=0.6)
        
        jagged_graph = axes.plot_line_graph(
            x_values=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9],
            y_values=[1, 4, 2, 5, 3, 4, 1, 3, 2],
            line_color=COLOR_PARAMS,
            add_vertex_dots=False
        )
        
        self.play(
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(COLOR_PARAMS),
            Write(mu_label),
            Write(sigma_label),
            Create(axes),
            Create(jagged_graph),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Lecture lines synchronized with script updates
        lecture_lines = [
            "Stat-Bot selects five random members from our population.",
            "We calculate the average value for this small sample.",
            "This average becomes a single point in our bin.",
            "We repeat this sampling process hundreds of times.",
            "The resulting collection is the Sampling Distribution of the Mean."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Sampling Experiment: Taking Averages", lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        STAT_BOT_COLOR = "#58C4DD"
        HIGHLIGHT_COLOR = "#FF8080"
        POP_COLOR = "#FFFFFF"
        BIN_COLOR = "#FFFFFF"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Visual: Stat-Bot selects five random members from our population.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(STAT_BOT_COLOR)
        
        # Population dots (Visual Anchor for 'Population')
        population = VGroup(*[Dot(radius=0.06, color=POP_COLOR) for _ in range(25)])
        self.place_in_area(population, "B3", "C5", scale_factor=1.0)
        # Randomize positions within area for a "cloud" look
        for dot in population:
            dot.shift(np.random.uniform(-0.6, 0.6, 3))
        self.add(population)
        
        # Stat-Bot (Visual Anchor for 'Robot Collector')
        stat_bot = VGroup(
            Square(side_length=0.7, fill_opacity=1, color=STAT_BOT_COLOR, stroke_width=2),
            Circle(radius=0.1, color=WHITE, fill_opacity=1).shift(UP*0.1 + LEFT*0.15),
            Circle(radius=0.1, color=WHITE, fill_opacity=1).shift(UP*0.1 + RIGHT*0.15),
        )
        self.place_at_grid(stat_bot, "B2")
        self.play(FadeIn(stat_bot))
        
        # Picking 5 dots - Highlighting the sample
        selected_indices = [0, 5, 10, 15, 20]
        selected_dots = VGroup(*[population[i] for i in selected_indices])
        
        self.play(
            stat_bot.animate.move_to(self.grid["B3"]),
            selected_dots.animate.set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR).scale(1.5),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Visual: We calculate the average value for this small sample.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR)
        
        # Display sample mean formula/value
        avg_math = Text("Sample Average (x̄) = 168", color=HIGHLIGHT_COLOR)
        self.place_in_area(avg_math, "D2", "D5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Write(avg_math))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Visual: This average becomes a single point in our bin.
        self.lecture[2].set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR)
        
        # Create a visual container (bin) for the sampling distribution
        bin_lines = VGroup(
            Line(self.grid["F2"], self.grid["F5"], color=BIN_COLOR, stroke_width=3), # Bottom
            Line(self.grid["E2"], self.grid["F2"], color=BIN_COLOR, stroke_width=3), # Left
            Line(self.grid["E5"], self.grid["F5"], color=BIN_COLOR, stroke_width=3)  # Right
        )
        self.play(Create(bin_lines))
        
        # Transform the selection/average into a single data point (dot)
        dot_from_avg = Dot(color=HIGHLIGHT_COLOR, radius=0.12)
        dot_from_avg.move_to(avg_math.get_center())
        
        self.play(
            FadeOut(avg_math),
            ReplacementTransform(selected_dots.copy(), dot_from_avg),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        
        # Drop the dot into the bin
        self.play(
            dot_from_avg.animate.move_to(self.grid["F3"] + UP*0.15),
            run_time=1
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Visual: We repeat this sampling process hundreds of times.
        self.lecture[3].set_color(POP_COLOR)
        
        # Fast sampling simulation to show volume of data
        sim_dots = VGroup()
        for _ in range(60):
            d = Dot(radius=0.07, color=HIGHLIGHT_COLOR)
            # Randomized spread within the bin boundaries
            offset_x = np.random.uniform(-1.4, 1.4)
            offset_y = np.random.uniform(0, 0.7)
            d.move_to(self.grid["F3"] + RIGHT*offset_x + UP*offset_y)
            sim_dots.add(d)
            
        self.play(
            LaggedStart(*[FadeIn(d, run_time=0.1) for d in sim_dots], lag_ratio=0.04),
            run_time=2.5
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # Visual: The resulting collection is the Sampling Distribution of the Mean.
        self.lecture[4].set_color(WHITE)
        
        # Final label for the new distribution
        final_label = Text("Sampling Distribution\nof the Mean", font_size=24, color=WHITE)
        self.place_in_area(final_label, "D2", "D5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Write(final_label))
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        title = "The Transformation: Emergence of the Bell Curve"
        lecture_lines = [
            "Watch the collection of sample averages grow over time.",
            "Even with messy source data, a pattern appears.",
            "The averages cluster around the true population mean.",
            "They form a smooth, bell-shaped Normal distribution.",
            "This magical transformation is the Central Limit Theorem."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_TOP = "#FFFFFF"
        COLOR_HIST = "#FF8080"
        COLOR_BELL = "#00FF00"
        COLOR_LINE = "#FFFF00"

        # Setup Axes for Top Plot
        top_axes = Axes(
            x_range=[0, 10, 1],
            y_range=[0, 5, 1],
            x_length=4,
            y_length=2,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "color": WHITE}
        )
        self.place_in_area(top_axes, 'B2', 'C6', scale_factor=0.8)

        # Setup Axes for Bottom Plot
        bottom_axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3, 1],
            y_range=[0, 1, 0.2],
            x_length=4,
            y_length=2.5,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "color": WHITE}
        )
        self.place_in_area(bottom_axes, 'D2', 'F6', scale_factor=0.8)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Show a jagged bimodal distribution plot at the top of the screen (#FFFFFF).
        self.lecture[0].set_color(COLOR_TOP)
        
        def bimodal_func(x):
            return 4 * (np.exp(-(x-2)**2) + np.exp(-(x-8)**2))
        
        bimodal_plot = top_axes.plot(bimodal_func, color=COLOR_TOP)
        top_label = Text("Original Population", font_size=16, color=COLOR_TOP)
        self.place_at_grid(top_label, 'B4', scale_factor=0.8) # Center label above plot

        self.play(Create(top_axes), Create(bimodal_plot), FadeIn(top_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # The bin of dots from the previous step starts to form a dense histogram (#FF8080).
        self.lecture[1].set_color(COLOR_HIST)
        
        # Create a "histogram" using bars to represent sample means distribution
        # For the animation, we'll draw many small bars.
        bars = VGroup()
        for i in range(21):
            x = -2 + i * 0.2
            h = np.exp(-x**2) * 0.8 # Normal distribution shape
            bar = Rectangle(
                width=0.15,
                height=h * bottom_axes.y_axis.unit_size,
                fill_color=COLOR_HIST,
                fill_opacity=0.7,
                stroke_width=0
            )
            bar.move_to(bottom_axes.c2p(x, 0), aligned_edge=DOWN)
            bars.add(bar)
        
        bottom_label = Text("Sample Means Distribution", font_size=16, color=COLOR_HIST)
        self.place_at_grid(bottom_label, 'D4', scale_factor=0.8)

        self.play(Create(bottom_axes), LaggedStart(*[GrowFromEdge(bar, DOWN) for bar in bars], lag_ratio=0.05), FadeIn(bottom_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # The averages cluster around the true population mean.
        # Overlay a smooth, glowing Bell Curve outline (#00FF00) onto the dot histogram.
        self.lecture[2].set_color(COLOR_BELL)
        
        bell_curve = bottom_axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-x**2) * 0.8, color=COLOR_BELL)
        # Add glow effect
        bell_glow = bell_curve.copy().set_stroke(width=8, opacity=0.3)
        
        self.play(Create(bell_curve), FadeIn(bell_glow))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # They form a smooth, bell-shaped Normal distribution.
        # Change the top jagged plot to a uniform distribution, while the bottom Bell Curve remains stable.
        self.lecture[3].set_color(COLOR_TOP)
        
        uniform_plot = top_axes.plot(lambda x: 2, color=COLOR_TOP)
        uniform_label = Text("Different Population (Uniform)", font_size=16, color=COLOR_TOP)
        self.place_at_grid(uniform_label, 'B4', scale_factor=0.8)

        self.play(
            ReplacementTransform(bimodal_plot, uniform_plot),
            ReplacementTransform(top_label, uniform_label)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # This magical transformation is the Central Limit Theorem.
        # Draw a vertical line through the peak of the Bell Curve to highlight its symmetry.
        self.lecture[4].set_color(COLOR_LINE)
        
        center_line = Line(
            bottom_axes.c2p(0, 0),
            bottom_axes.c2p(0, 1),
            color=COLOR_LINE,
            stroke_width=4
        )
        mean_label = Text("μ", color=COLOR_LINE, font_size=32)
        self.place_at_grid(mean_label, 'F4', scale_factor=0.8) # Position near bottom of axis

        self.play(Create(center_line), Write(mean_label))
        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Data from shared state/coordination
        title_text = "The Law of Large Numbers (Sample Size n)"
        lecture_lines = [
            "Small samples produce wide, short distributions.",
            "This spread reflects higher uncertainty in our estimate.",
            "Increasing n makes the distribution taller and thinner.",
            "This results in much higher precision around the mean.",
            "We quantify this spread using the Standard Error formula.",
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_WIDE = "#FFDAB9"  # n=2
        COLOR_NARROW = "#87CEFA" # n=50
        COLOR_PRECISION = "#00FF00"
        COLOR_FORMULA = "#FFFF00"
        COLOR_HIGHLIGHT = "#FFFFFF"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        axes_left = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3, 1], y_range=[0, 1, 0.5],
            x_length=2.5, y_length=1.5,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "color": GREY}
        )
        self.place_in_area(axes_left, "C2", "D3", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        curve_wide = axes_left.plot(
            lambda x: np.exp(-0.5 * (x / 1.2)**2) / (1.2 * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)),
            color=COLOR_WIDE
        )
        # Fix: Replaced MathTex with Text to avoid FileNotFoundError: 'latex'
        label_n2 = Text("n=2", color=COLOR_WIDE, font_size=24)
        self.place_at_grid(label_n2, "B2", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(COLOR_WIDE))
        self.play(Create(axes_left), Create(curve_wide), Write(label_n2))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        arrow_wide = DoubleArrow(
            axes_left.c2p(-1.5, 0.1), axes_left.c2p(1.5, 0.1),
            color=COLOR_HIGHLIGHT, buff=0, tip_length=0.1
        )
        text_uncertainty = Text("Uncertain", color=COLOR_HIGHLIGHT, font_size=16)
        self.place_at_grid(text_uncertainty, "E2", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(COLOR_HIGHLIGHT))
        self.play(GrowFromCenter(arrow_wide), FadeIn(text_uncertainty))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        axes_right = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3, 1], y_range=[0, 1, 0.5],
            x_length=2.5, y_length=1.5,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "color": GREY}
        )
        self.place_in_area(axes_right, "C4", "D5", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        curve_narrow = axes_right.plot(
            lambda x: np.exp(-0.5 * (x / 0.4)**2) / (0.4 * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)),
            color=COLOR_NARROW
        )
        # Fix: Replaced MathTex with Text to avoid FileNotFoundError: 'latex'
        label_n50 = Text("n=50", color=COLOR_NARROW, font_size=24)
        self.place_at_grid(label_n50, "B4", scale_factor=1.0)

        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(COLOR_NARROW))
        self.play(Create(axes_right), Create(curve_narrow), Write(label_n50))

        title_text = "The Magic of the Central Limit Theorem"

        formula = Text(

        plot_group = VGroup(axes, curve)

outline.topic: The Magic of the Central Limit Theorem: Finding Order in Chaos
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students in introductory statistics or data science

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of a Population vs. Sample
sections.content: Establish the foundational vocabulary. We define a 'Population' as the entire group and a 'Sample' as a subset. Introduce the 'Population Mean' (μ) and 'Standard Deviation' (σ). Visualize various non-normal distributions (uniform, skewed, and bimodal) to show that real-world data is rarely a perfect bell curve.
sections.example: Imagine a digital forest inhabited by thousands of 'Data-Monsters' of various heights. Some are tiny, some are giants, and their height distribution looks like a jagged mountain range, not a smooth curve.

sections.title: The Sampling Experiment: Taking Averages
sections.content: Introduce the process of 'Sampling Distribution.' We don't look at individual monster heights; instead, we take a small group (n=5), calculate their average height, and plot that single point. We repeat this process hundreds of times. Visually, show the dots falling into a new chart below the original distribution.
sections.example: A robot named 'Stat-Bot' grabs 5 random monsters, averages their heights, and drops a marble into a glass bin representing that average. It repeats this 1,000 times.

sections.title: The Transformation: Emergence of the Bell Curve
sections.content: This is the 'Aha!' moment. As the number of samples increases, the 'bin of marbles' begins to change shape. Even though the original monster forest was jagged and weird, the distribution of their *sample means* starts to look like a symmetric Bell Curve (Normal Distribution). Demonstrate that this happens regardless of the original shape.
sections.example: An animation shows the jagged 'Mountain Range' distribution at the top, while the 'Stat-Bot's' marble bin at the bottom morphs into a glowing, smooth Bell Curve.

sections.title: The Law of Large Numbers (Sample Size n)
sections.content: Explain the role of the sample size 'n'. If n is small (e.g., n=2), the curve is wide and messy. As n increases (usually n ≥ 30), the curve becomes thinner and taller. This introduces the formula for Standard Error: σ/√n. Show how larger samples lead to higher precision.
sections.example: Compare two bins: one where Stat-Bot picks 2 monsters (wide, blurry curve) and one where it picks 50 monsters (a very sharp, narrow spike centered exactly at the true population mean).

sections.title: Mathematical Definition & Key Properties
sections.content: Formalize the theorem: For any population with mean μ and standard deviation σ, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a Normal Distribution N(μ, σ²/n) as n becomes large. Emphasize three points: 1. Center is μ. 2. Spread is σ/√n. 3. Shape is Normal.
sections.example: A graphic overlay displays the formula: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n), with arrows pointing to the visual elements of the bell curve created by the Data-Monsters.

sections.title: Application: Why It Matters in the Real World
sections.content: Explain that the CLT is the 'Superpower' of statistics. It allows us to make confident predictions about a whole population by looking at samples, even if we don't know the population's original distribution shape. This is the basis for opinion polls, medical trials, and quality control.
sections.example: A quality control engineer at a lightbulb factory doesn't need to test every bulb until it breaks. By testing small batches (samples), the CLT allows them to calculate the exact probability that the entire day's production is high quality.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of a Population vs. Sample
lecture_lines: A population represents every individual in a group.
A sample is just a small portion of them.
We describe groups using means and standard deviations.

Transform the cluster into a jagged, bimodal distribution curve (#FFFF00).

storyboard.title: The Sampling Experiment: Taking Averages
lecture_lines: Stat-Bot selects five random members from our population.
We calculate the average value for this small sample.
This average becomes a single point in our bin.
We repeat this sampling process hundreds of times.
The resulting collection is the Sampling Distribution of the Mean.
animations: Animate a 'Stat-Bot' figure [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/robot.svg] selecting 5 random shapes (#FF8080).
Calculate their average and display it as a dot (#FF8080).
Drop many dots into a bin to form a histogram (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The Transformation: Emergence of the Bell Curve
lecture_lines: Observe how the population's starting shape is extremely jagged.
But the collection of sample averages forms a pattern.
It settles into a smooth, symmetric bell-shaped curve.
The same shape appears regardless of the starting distribution.
This transformation is the heart of the Central Limit Theorem.
animations: Show the bin from section 2 rapidly filling with dots (#FF8080).
Highlight a pattern emerging from the dense dot cluster (#FFFFFF).
Draw a vertical line through the center labeled 'μ' (#FFFF00).
Overlay a glowing Bell Curve outline (#00FF00) onto the histogram.
Flash the Bell Curve and text 'Central Limit Theorem' (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The Law of Large Numbers (Sample Size n)
lecture_lines: Larger sample sizes create narrower and taller curves.
The spread is determined by the Standard Error formula.
Every curve centers exactly at the true population mean.
animations: Display a wide, short curve (n=2, #FFDAB9) on the left.
Highlight the wide base of the curve with arrows (#FFFFFF).
Display a narrow, tall curve (n=50, #87CEFA) on the right.
Shrink the width of the tall curve to show precision (#00FF00).
Display the formula 'SE = σ / √n' (#FFFF00) in center.

storyboard.title: Mathematical Definition & Key Properties
lecture_lines: Mathematically, the sample mean follows a Normal distribution.
Its center is exactly the population mean, mu.
The spread is the standard deviation divided by sqrt(n).
We write this as N(mu, sigma squared over n).
This holds true if the sample size is large enough.
animations: Display the CLT formula 'x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n)' (#FFFF00).
Highlight 'μ' and align it with the curve's peak (#00FF00).
Highlight 'σ²/n' and show it controlling curve width (#58C4DD).
Animate 'N' expanding into 'Normal Distribution' text (#FFFFFF).
Show 'n → ∞' as the curve becomes perfectly smooth (#FFFFFF).

lecture_lines: The CLT allows predictions without knowing the population shape.
